title: Arlo and the Great Food Journey
markdown:
The sun burst through Arlo’s window, a brilliant bold gold. Birdsong trilled a lively tune. Today felt special. Arlo practically bounced out of bed, a kinetic burst. “Today’s the day!” His bridge plans were absolutely perfect, meticulously sketched on his workbench. And his lunch — a true masterpiece, a tart baked with extra love by the renowned Auntie Noor. He dashed, fingers itching for his sturdy lunchbox. Click! The latch sprang open.

Empty. His magnificent tart was gone. His jaw dropped.

“No! My tart!”

Tansy the squirrel zoomed past the window, a blur, tail twitching. She skidded on the garden path, chattering distress. Her prize acorn — the plumpest, smoothest she had ever found — was gone from its careful store.

“My best nut!” Tiny paws scrabbled at empty earth. A tremor ran through Arlo. A puzzle with two missing pieces and no courtesy note.

“A puzzle, you say?” Auntie Noor’s voice came from the kitchen, warm, apron dusted as if a small snow had visited. “A missing tart? A vanished acorn? Come, little builders and collectors. The world does not take things without reason.”

She led them to a table by the sunlit window. Golden-brown crumbs: the tart’s last evidence.

“Observe. Your tart did not sprout wings. It was eaten. How did it leave the box?” A flour-dusted finger toward Arlo’s mouth. “Those tools. First tools of transformation. Sharp. They bite, tear, chomp.” A tap on his tongue. “This mashes and mixes. Big pieces into little bits. Much smaller.”

Arlo chewed an imaginary crumb with dramatic flair. It felt, in his mind, softer, more willing to travel.

“But what happens to the small bits?” His builder brain clicked. Tansy forgot the catastrophe long enough to twitch her nose. This was better than frantic searching.

Auntie Noor’s smile widened. “That, my dears, is where the real journey of food begins.” She beckoned them outside, steps light. Morning air wonderfully cool and crisp, faint scent of blooming roses. Dewdrops sparkled like tiny diamonds on every blade and petal. They followed a faint almost invisible trail of the tiniest crumbs from the lunchbox, past the grand old oak, toward Auntie Noor’s lush garden. A small shiny beetle, shell like polished obsidian, scuttled over a particularly fine crumb, nudged it, nibbled with tiny precise movements.

“Look!” Tansy chirped, pointing. “It’s eating the crumbs! Making them even smaller!”

Further along, near a patch of wonderfully soft dark earth, a plump earthworm, segmented body glistening, wriggled past, seemingly drawn by the faint scent of apple and spice, toward the scattered tart bits.

“It’s all breaking down,” Arlo realized, understanding dawning. “The tart… it’s becoming part of them. Not just gone. Traveling.” Dispersing. Transforming. A miniature adventure that did not require wings.

Auntie Noor’s quiet satisfaction. “Your teeth did the first big work. Then other helpers — beetle, worm, and the tiny workers inside you — take the pieces. Energy. Building. Bridges, perhaps. A nest against the wind. Digestion.”

Arlo pictured golden tart making a beetle’s shell surer, a worm’s burrow deeper, Tansy’s next dash possible. The acorn, too, would fuel somebody’s flight or dig. The mystery loosened, not into a sermon about tapestries, but into crumbs with jobs.

“So my tart is still here.” A grin chased the panic.

“In a different form. Food’s adventure.”

Tansy chattered agreement, calmer. Her acorn had a purpose even if it was no longer under her paw.

Arlo skipped toward the workbench, lunchbox swinging, empty and honest. He would draw the crumb-trail beside the bridge plans, a second kind of span: mouth to middle to muscle. Auntie Noor was already dusting flour for another tart, because journeys, she said, go better with a spare. Tansy sat on the windowsill and considered a lesser acorn, which is squirrel for starting again. The beetle, uninterested in speeches, finished the last flake and went on being a beetle, slightly more energetic than before.
